prayer.text: Saint Wolfgang of Regensburg, pray for us.

cues.text: A Count's Son from Swabia
Wolfgang was born about the year 934 into a family of Swabian counts, in what is now Germany.
As a boy of seven he had a priest for a tutor, and later he studied at the great monastic school of Reichenau.
There he formed a strong friendship with Henry, the brother of the Bishop of Würzburg.
When Henry went on to Würzburg, Wolfgang followed him to attend the lectures of the Italian grammarian Stephen of Novara.
Teacher at Trier, Monk at Einsiedeln
In 956 Henry became Archbishop of Trier and called his friend to join him.
Wolfgang taught in the cathedral school and worked to reform the archdiocese, though his efforts met with enmity.
At Trier he came to know the reforming monastery of St. Maximin, and there he met Ramwold, the teacher of Adalbert of Prague.
When Henry died in 964, Wolfgang entered the order of St. Benedict at the Abbey of Einsiedeln in Switzerland.
St. Ulrich ordained him a priest in 968.
In the quiet of the cloister, a teacher became a monk.
Sent to the Magyars
After their defeat at the battle of the Lechfeld in 955, the pagan Magyars settled in ancient Pannonia, and as long as they remained unconverted they threatened the empire.
At the request of St. Ulrich and the desire of Emperor Otto the Great, Wolfgang was sent to evangelize them, according to the annals of his abbey.
Other missionaries followed from Bishop Piligrim of Passau, but Wolfgang's own mission was cut short.
When Bishop Michael of Regensburg died on September 23, 972, Piligrim obtained the emperor's appointment of Wolfgang in his place.
Wolfgang became bishop at Christmas that year.
A monk who had entered the cloister was called next to a mission, and then to a bishop's chair.
A Bishop Who Taught and Reformed
As bishop, Wolfgang became the tutor of Emperor Henry II, who learned from him the principles of a saintly and energetic life.
His pupils also included Gisela, who later became the wife of Stephen I of Hungary .
The man once sent to evangelize Hungary taught its future queen.
He gave the ancient Abbey of St. Emmeram abbots of its own again, ending the long custom of the bishops holding it for themselves.
In 975 he called the monk Ramwold from Trier to lead it.
He also reformed the convents of Obermünster and Niedermünster, giving them as a model his own foundation of St. Paul at Mittelmünster.
Generous to the Empire and the Poor
Wolfgang met the emperor's plan for a new Diocese of Prague, carved from his own, with what the Catholic Encyclopedia calls "genuine episcopal generosity."
Adalbert became its first bishop.
Wolfgang also served the empire faithfully, attending imperial diets and accompanying Emperor Otto II on his campaign to Paris in 978.
Yet he never laid aside the monk.
He wore the Benedictine habit, lived an austere life, and showed a special concern for the poor.
The Hermit and the Hunter
Later in his life, Wolfgang withdrew to a solitary place in the wilderness, now the Lake of St. Wolfgang in Austria.
The Catholic Encyclopedia says this was apparently because of a political dispute.
A hunter found him and brought him back to Regensburg.
In 994 he was travelling down the Danube toward Pöchlarn when he fell ill at the village of Pupping.
At his request he was carried into the chapel of St. Othmar, and there he died on October 31, 994.
His friends Count Aribo of Andechs and Archbishop Hartwich of Salzburg took his body up the Danube to Regensburg, where he was buried in the crypt of St. Emmeram.
Miracles were reported at his grave, and in 1052 he was canonized.
The Axe, the Wolf, and the Legacy
Tradition holds that Wolfgang chose the site of his cell by throwing his axe into the thicket and building where it fell.
The axe is still shown in the market town of St. Wolfgang, which grew up on that spot.
A later legend relates that he forced the devil to help him build a church.
In one retelling, the devil's price was the first soul to enter, and when the church was finished, a hunted wolf ran through the door first.
Soon after his death, many churches chose Wolfgang as their patron, and towns took his name.
He is the patron saint of Regensburg.
He shows us still that reform begins quietly, with a school, a rule of prayer, and an open hand to the poor.
October 31 is better known for another feast.
Those who keep this one honor a bishop who built up the Church by teaching, by serving, and by giving way when the Church needed more.
